INTERESTISG LETTER FROM MR. JAMES
WINSTAN LEY.

31r. .John Gandy. 31arrington, has received another letter from Mr. Winstanley, who left War- rington with hi,: family last year. It ie dated Salem, Oregon, March 111th, PN/. We give the bulk of it no fOHOWS; . I •

I received your bundle of papers this week for which I thank you much. I missed one week and I could not tell what was the matter. I would sooner ! miss a meld than the " Examiner." We are having lovely weather ; for two mont he we have hint all sunshine with just one day a rain; it to indeed One. This, in my opium, is the hest part of the year. There aro no house Hies to torment you, although I have seen more mosquitos this week than I have van since WO came here, yet there are not sufficient of them to he inethlesome. I was talking tuna old Oregonian this and lie earl ---" This weather , heats Oregon, and Oregon beats the world." That is the way they speak of this, climate, and yet with it all your humble servant has had to quit work again. I have been sick again with more of those stupid boile and an attack of catarrh, but I am better, and I shall start work again to-marrow. I expect all the rest are very well. The peach—and in fact all the fruit trees— are bursting out in bloom; the peach especially is very pretty. I am expecting a youth from Birmingham to eome and live with us. lie has written me, and says lie in Coming oat this summer. Ile lo one of Mrs. Winstenley's cousins' children. Ile hns been living on a farm some years, so I expect he will do me some service. I have promised him a home until he can make one for himself. .

What do vou think of my speculation now when : I tell you I had 1011 dollars per acre offeied for my place on Friday I tell you it is very gratifying to mo to find it has doubled the price in six months. Ida not want to sell. I want to live on the place ; we all like it better every week ; nature seems to unfold new beauties every day. I have planted out 1,000 strawberries and MO fruit trees, besides raspberries and currants and black- berries ; so it is quite possible we shall get a few berries this year ; at least I hope we shall get as many as we require for home use. We are very , short of that sort of thing at present, as we did not have a chance of preserving or canning much last year, but I guess there will be more canned this

1 We have not hoard anything.. of our piano, or of : the good ship "Thos. S. Stowe; it is now a month . overdue. lam afraid there is something wrong or we should have heard something before this. I often wonder what you are doing. I started to write this at :seven o'clock this morning ; that would be nearly half-past three with you. Since then I have been to church and school, and then lunch makes it three o'clock. We all had a walk in the woods to see how much wood the men have cut, as they are paid 1 dollar per cord (which is Bft. by 4by 4), cutup and staeked. We gathered wild flowers and ferns. Too should see some of the ,• snakes, how pretty they are as they wriggle along I with their tongues out ; none of as are afraid of them, even my wife almost touched one with her foot ; they are so common. I have not got all my wheat sown yet, hut I expect to get it all in this week. I have been keep- ing one part of the land to pasture the cow and calf. but it is now ploughed up and the cow has to pas- ture in the woods along with other people's stock. of which there are plenty. All woods are free which are not fenced, and sometimes the COI. wander four or live miles away from their homes in search of pastures fresh, and back again each milking time. night and morning. My boy Harry starts school to-morrow (Monday). The school has been closed six mont Its ; just fancy, six months' vacation each year! No wonder at the boys out here going to school until they are 16 years, and then they are not so good as they ough; to be at 12 years old. They run wild half their time and forget all they have learnt. That is one the evils of Free Education. Some day I will write up a letter on the school question, if my health permits, hut at present it is quite is task to think and more no to write, but I hope to he better by-and-bye. Last night I was dreaming you had been over here, and you insisted on my going hack home with you, and we had some fine times on the way, I can tell you. All my people are well, for which lam ' thankful. , I have read Whitham's letters with interest. There is a lot of truth in them about English goods, &co It is the same at Salem. but Ido not think he is very wise to tight too much against the people he is (olive with.

THE EXAMINER.
SATLI<DAY. APRIL O. 1889.

Mn. HENRY BROADHURST, M.P., has not sum ceedeil in carrying the motion which he made in the House of Commons on Tuesday evening. It wee to the effect that the chronic poverty of great numbero of the people living in the larger cities and towns is a danger to the State, and " calls for the instant attention of the Govermnont to remedial measures by which the depopulation of the agricultural districts may be checked, and the eongestion of the groat centres of population relieved." It woo hm much, it eeems, to expect the present Government. to support the motion. The Ti mien have a rooted dislike to the discusanion of topits of thin kind, for they expose the defects of the Ministry, and the supineness and 'selfishness of the privileged classes. When Mr. BROADHURST remarked that " leaseholds, ground rent, and in fact the whole subject of land law reform must be dealt with in any question affecting the housing of the working people in large towns," the obser- vation was greeted with derisive laughter on the tort of the Ministorialisto Let the working classes note the meaning of this insolent attitude. It semis that the Tories aro now, as over, wedded to a barbanms land system, and that they will do nothing, situ they are compelled, in the way of providing a real remedy. They canmA even possess their souls in patience whilst a repreeen- Wive of working-men exponmbi his views and the views of millions of working-men throughout the kingdom. It in all very well for full-fed land-owners in the House of Commons to troop in after dinner, and sneer at the idea of bad land laws havi ll g anything to do with the removal ,if agricultural labourers to our large towns. It suite them to " Riot and he thankful," for they :ea, maid hi rust, and have every reason to be thankful. Rot it is quite otherwise with three aim are suffering—with the men who find it ot impossible to get a bit of land 14 their we,awl who eannot see their way to any end lot the workhouse, if they attempt to bring up a family in twelve shillings a week. Is it any wonder that they tramp into towns to compete with thousands of others who, like themeolvee, are w.a•li in :mil week out in the borders of starve- :- It in suggested that land might be oiler the, Allotments Act ; but the Act inocloTy. --- A London correspondent ears:—" The new Earl of Carlisle is a strong teetotaller, and so is Lady Carlisle. Since he has had the management of the estates as (me .4 the trustees, he has closed all the public-houses 1.1 the property. The cellar at Castle Howard contained some of the best home-brewed ' ale in Enghuni, and the brewhouses were famous everywhere, hut they have been entirely destroyed and the vats emptied."

Lord Aberdare and Mr. Justice Grantham are not having it all their own way in their comments on the working of the Welsh Sunday Closing Act. . On Tuoiday a meeting of eleven hualred Rh. ondda Valley miners o.ssed unanimous resolutions in favour of the continuance of the Act, and supfort- ing au official inquiry into its operation. These I miners may be presumed to know something of the subject, and they are in a majority.

Edward Moore, who was going to visit some friends in London, has narrated his experiences of the accident, and the following is a digest of what he says : —" About 200 cards beyond renisone station we were startled by a heivy oscillation, followed by a m.t fear- ful jolting, which knocked as all about the carriage. hats, and lags Were all Palau' inn heap on the floor of the compartment, and the passengers with me—four Southport gentlemen—were or shaken that for short time we could scarcely stand or move, I picked up my scar umbrella, bui the silk hat been torn , away unit cut with a knife. In the confusion which I prevailed each pot on a wrong hat, and the gentleman nearest the door opened it and got out. Our carriage I was not locked. It was tilted on its side at an angle of! from 30 to 35 degrees. We all got out of the train as soon as we could, and the first thing I did was to bump against a portion of the rail, whiell was in an upright position, and which nearly caused me to fall to the ground. A scene of the most extraordinary confusion and horror presented itself. There was one carriage! noticed almost. at right angles to the line. Theend of it had been jammed la. and the next carriage had been forced right into it. The Coroner's inquiry into the cause of death of Barnes was concluded at Penistone on Mau lay. From the evidence it appeared that the accident was due to the snapping of the leading axle of the engine, in cense- quenee of a flaw which could not have been discovered except by destroying the wheels. The engine was built in 1865, and it was stated that area then it had travelled over 600,000 cues. After a short consultation, the jury bound that the death of Barnes was the result of an accident, and expressed the opinion that for that acci- dent the Railway Company were in no any to blame. A STORE SERIOUS. DISASTER AVERT.. In the course of Tuesday afternoon Major General • Hutchinson, the inspector appointed by the Board of Trade to examine into the cause of the accident, opened his inquiry at Penistone railway station, The statements given before him confirmed previous information that a terrible disaster was only averted by the presenceof mind of a signalman and the driver and stoker of the excur- sion train. The mail train from London was approach- ing the place at full speed when the accident happened, and although checked by the signals thrown up against him, before the driver knew what was the matter he had struck the tender of the disabled train, which lay , across the metals on which be wila travelling. Several of the Warrington passengers have eidumentrld ill thrms of admiration on the presence of mind of those who averted what would have been an appalline calamity. \VAIUUiGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

Wonder of wonders—a Tory Prime Minister was on Thursday evening defeated in the House of Lords. Lord Salisbury tried to secure the post of Chairman of Committees for Lord Balfour of llurleigh. It carries with it a nice picking of 1:2;100 a year. It was generally believed that Lord Morley. by his tact, training, and experience, was I,est qualified for the tnut. He was proposed for it by Lend Granville, and he was carried by a majority f In. The majority nmy be small bat it has certainly made Lord Salisbury look small.

Th"re is rejoicing over the letters from Mr. Stanley as one who was lost and is found again. ' He disappeared from the ken of civilisation from I Juno ISS7 to. August lif last year. Ho went in search of Liv 11l gstone, and found him, and he has hound Mein Pasha. Dein is like Livingstone—he is not disposed to leave :dries. Stanley and his men have suffered terribly, but endurance and heroism have triumphed. The great explorer is again tempting fortune by piercing the heart of the Dark Continent. May he come forth alive and well, and permit his countrymen ti) see his tam! Mr. Briellaugh is still "death on pensions." It is due to his activity and tact that there is an end of what are known a.s perpetual pensions :and now he is raising an arm to strike against political pen- sions. Ho has brought in a bill, (backed by Mr. Dillwyn and Mr. Summers ) which has for its object the m 1,0.144 the Political Offices Pensions Act of I*l9. He pro's'ses to spare existing holders, for 1 he wants his bill to pass, and, if it do pass, there ! will be no further extension of the system of draw- ing a big pension, of ter drawing a big salary, for doing work which has,sometimos, been ridiculously small.

In the French Chamber, on Thursday evening. the prosecution of General Boulanger was decided upon by 3.13 votes to 199. But the brave General has "cot and run"; he is at Brussels out of harnis way. This has disgusted some of his followers. One of his Radical supporters, M.Michelin, writes : —" When a man is at the head of a movement he should remain at his post and not desert the army of which he is the chief. He must allow himself ! to be imprisoned like Bathes, or shot like Delos- close. To my mind the Bou/angist Committee no longer exists: at any rate I no longer belong to it.' It looks as if Boulangism will before long be a burst bubble.

In the House of Commons, on Thursday even- ing, an attack was made by the Liberals on the bad finance of the Tories in seeking to raise money for the navy by spewing, so to speak, upon their successors. Mr. Childers, who led the Opposition, said that of the kl 7,000,000 to be raised no less than 25,000,000 were to be provided by the next !Parliament. This means that Liberals are. as usual, to be called on to pay Tory debts. Mr. Gladstone joined in the debate, and thoroughly exposed this • "deremy-diddling." Mr. Childers did not carry , his amendment, nut it is significant that the Government majority was only 33. It looks like I the beginning of the end.

" The union of the Unionists " is a noble senti- ment, for dot's it not MOllll sacrificing everything to maintain the grandeur and glory of an empire on which the min never sets ? Of ammoe it does ; and yet there is a rift within thehite. John Bright dies and Unionists of all shades in Commons and in Lords express reverence for his memory. He loaves a son who is a Unionist—John Albert ' I bright, and what more fitting —more beautifully I appropriate —than that the Cnionist son should take the seat which the father left vacant ? But the Unionists who are Conservatives suddenly : demur. They want to make 101131 Bright's , seat a Tory seat ; reverence for the dead, and affection for " the union of the Unionists" vanish at the prospect of A Tory gain. Alas ! and alas! Great is Cant, and Humbug is his ' brother.

MT SI:TON-KARR sought to get the Govern- ment out if a difficulty in dealing with the motion by proposing, as an amendment, the adoption of 0111, well-devised scheme of State col. misatioa." Hut properly speaking it was not an amendment, for if the member for St. Helens thinks colonisa- tiohiit practical remedy for congestiim in air large towns, there was Ho reanon why he should not urge his plan whilst at the same time sums•rting Mr. Ilsomilirmifs motion. But Mr. BROADHURST was to he got rid of as a traiblesinne representa- tive of working-menc and, seeing the game which has soil piece I, it would he well if the working- men "ISt. Helens would get rid, at the earliest opportunity, of the mischievous member who mis- represents them. Is there any evidence, we would ask, of a desire on the part if our labouring pop- ulation to be shipped of wholesale and dumped down in the wildernesses of the colonies ? And if there is no such desire, would Mr. SETON-K Ann send them out of the country whether they will or no ? Tories talk much at times about the hive of our native land : but it would seem to lie patrio- tism of The SITTON-KA RD type to show one's love of country by fleeing from it when reform is in the air. We havo no objection to giving further assistance to those who desire to emigrate, but we do object to State colonisation as a substit mute for just land laws. "If," says the member for St. Helens, "there is a doubt now as to the agricul- : tura' resources of the country being able to keep the industrial population, how will it be possible for tie ~ resources to maintain the population in a few years time, when it is increased by seven or eight millions ? " It will certainly not be , possible, if we lie in the rut in which we have floundered so long, and in which Mr. Same-Kane and his friends would keep us. Let our land 'laws he reformed is the direction indicatml, and we venture to say there will be plenty of work! at home for our growing population. Lord Daunt, who is not temally rash in his estimates, has stated that the land id this country might be , made to yield double its present produce. There I is at least half of the land not properly drained, and it never will be properly drained whilst it is I , tied up by the dead hand of the aristocrat who has thought more of keeping his acres together ' than of bringing them under good cultivation. But the spirit of reform is abroad; the Sarofi- KA RDS,iind GILDHRT Ti MARNA LLS,DiId the EDWARDS- Mimsao may stay its progress for a brief period a hut the period will be brief. The masses are growing in intelligence as they are growing in numbers ; sad, despite the obstruction and trick- ery, and stupidity with which they ore assailed, they cannot for much longer be defrauded of their inheritance.

I Ton Annual Iteimrt of the Medical Officer of Health for Warril igton is always carefully prepared awl exhaustive. De. GORNALL takes a pride in doing his work thoronghly ; in his record he noth- ing extenuates nor sots down aught in malice, whilst he makes it Ida business, when desirable, to pointout the weak spots in the sanitary condition of the town. Pr 'greets in matters of sanitation is exceedingly slow: there is agent deal of ignorance, mid not a little stu;iiility to ',intend with, and a town in therefore favoured which has a Medical Officer of Health who is in advance of the times, and an Ahler.nan as Chairman of Cournittee who has for very in toy ye ire TAN4IOII3Iy 110VOLA him- self to saidtary work. One of the most interesting features of the R lyirt in that relating to the population of the borough. Warrington is growing, but it is not growing quite as feat as was supposed. If the population had increased in these later years as it did between 1671 and ISPH, the total to-day would have been 51,001—that magical number which enables a country town to become a town county. The special poll taken in May last showed that the number of inhabitants was 47,325. It is now, mundly speaking, 40,000. Turn- ing to another important point we find that the rate of mortality for the year is 2011 per 1,000. This is rather over the average of the country ; but it is something gained that the deaths in Warrington for bae4 are 2.9 per 1,0(Y) lower than 1807. Indeed, considering that the town has suffered, and still suffers, from an epidemic of scarlet fever, it is gratifying to learn that the death rate is so low. There were AA many as 00 deathe from scarlet fever in ISM, as against one only in 1807, and none in ISkri 'Cr 1,446. Dr. ' GOKNALL remarks, in his letter to the Local Government Board, that " the dittoes° has boon entirely confined to the classes earning weekly wages.' Following up thin obitervation, it would be well if the Sanitary Committee would take moans to ascertain whether the epidemic has been in the main confined to particular localities and particular streets. It in possible—it is, in fact, probable--that the effluvia from the Intercepting DepCite may have to do with the development of scarlet and other fevers and if this be found to be the case, it ia a matter ,if course to say that the Sanitary Committee will see to it that the beat and speediest means are taken to render the depots harmless and inoffensive. There is need, it would aoem,for " a suitable map of the borough,so necessary for statistical and other sanitary pur- poses"; but it into he hoped there will be no need to refer to such a requirement in the next Report. The Infectiona Diseases Hospital hoe proved a great boon to the town. It can hardly be doubted that had it not been for this valuable institution there would have been a serious outbreak of smallpox—such as there was last year in many Lancashire towns. As it was, each rape was isolated as soon as it was discovered, and, thanks to the prompt and vigorous measures of the Medical Officer of Health, the diem.° was quickly stamped out. Dr. GONNALL LI supported at the hospital by an admirable matron, and it will interest the taxpayer to know that, compared with other inatitutii ins of a like kind, the War- rington Fever Hospital is economically mumiged.

Kerr, Jones, McGuire, Leonard, Bradshaw, and Bradburn, forwards. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER FREE WANDERERS. The return fixture between these organizations took place on Saturday, when the Free Wanderers paid their annual visit to Warrington. The first match resulted in an easy victory for our local team by two goals. Although Saturday's contest was looked to as a foregone conclusion for the Warringtonians, a fair attendance WWI recorded. Both sides were representative, although Speakman, Frank Tamer, and Jolley were absent from the Warring.knn ranks. The Rolle skipper neon the choke of ends, and elected to defend the pavilion goal. Nevins met the kick off with a reply to the half way flag, where from a line-out I the Warrington forwards rushed the oval to their oppon- ent,' quarter flag. Barns received a pass from Antrobus but a hasty shot at goal only registered a armor . No relief was brought from the drop out, Nevins respond- ing, Goldthorpe had a kick charged, and matter:: again assumed: a gloomy aspect for the Wanderers. lirand

The application of the principles of biology to t he A ItATE.PATER. phenomena of soviet, militical, and religious life is a Runcorn, April 301, 18E19. marked feature of modern thought, anti one prOdae- DVI. of much interesting speculation. The names of Spencer. flagella. and Drummond, will occur an conspicuous examples of this mole of thinking. The impetus given to the world of thought by the writings of Mr. Darwin is not yet exhausted. Few I bociks have hail anything approaching the intio- ence upon !heir ago as that exerted by the "Origin nil peie'2 Er 1 the views expressed Illereill Dar- i wits was ounewhat indebted to his gmmlfat her, and his grandfather was under obligation to Lamarck. I Alfred Russell Wallace, also, ban ample claim to be I regarded as co-discoverer of 0111C11 that is generally thought of as being distinctively Darwinian. But it , is the old tale. lienius takes over to itself the in-1 distinct ideas, and imperfect eolleeptioll4, of a pre- vious age, and invests them with life and imm rtali- ty. Anil this is the imperishable service Darwin did for biological wiener. Another genius will some day, we timid not, render to tint future a ser- vice like that rendered by Darwin to the present. then will be heard less abort the need for Agnos- ticism. and more about the loving wisdom of the I Eternal. Until then, the wheat and the tares will ! grow together in the worlds harvest field of ' thought. The hold of Darwin on the common mind is no- where 11111 l e clearly shown than in the general use of the well known phrase " Survival of the fittest." This formula requires receiving with caution. Its magnificent comprehensiveness is a snare. It may mean anything, everything, nothing. From the fact that countless multi: udes of organisms come into existence only to immediately decay and die, it is inferred that those whirl, survive are the fittest, the hest adapted to life. Anil thus a law le, net lip hav- ing universal application. Whether, in a stricaly scientific sense, it is entitled to the dignity of a law will not be here discussed, except so far as its application to civilized society is concerned. Do the littest survive? Do the unfit die off? Certainly not acconling to the Darwinian notion of fitness. The progtess of medical science is. among other things, bringing about incre..tvl facilities for the survi oil of the unlit. Men who, had they lived fifty .years age would have lost hope, are enaliled by the science of to-day to indefinitely prolong their lives At the base of British society are a million paupers. They survive at the cost of about I:10 per head. Do they survive because they are the fittest? At the apex of society is a parasitical aristocracy maintained in idle luxury by the hard hands and busy brains of the sons of toil. Is this tease of the survival of the fittest "? Then observe the effect of war on aociety. The young and able-bodied, vigorous in thought and action, are drafted off to be slaughtered by machine guns, while the weak and incapable are left at home to propagate their like. Again, the birth rate is much higher among the poor and destitute than among the well-to-de The unfit generate the fastest, nor does the death rate practically alter the proportion. From a con- sideration of modern civilisation, an unbiassed mind might easily infer that the unfittest survive. Granted that the fittest survive, who are they? What are their characteristics? Why should we endeavour to regulate society by hazy generalize-, tions drawn from natures lower, immeasurably lower, than our own? Men are bound together by a thousand links of which the lower creation knows nothing. Society is not, has no right to be, a com- mon lodging-house where the weakest are remorse. leanly forced to the wall. This law is too individual- istic to be socially trite. If the drunkard weakling and profligate died off without effecting the coming generation then Society would become speedily purified. But this is not no. humanity in one— one in origin, one in destiny. We cannot live to ourselves, we dare not die to ourselves. The Cause of one is the Cause of all. After much weariness and sorrow, and severe discipline, Humanity will, one day struggle into the light, the peace, the ineffable happiness of God's kingdom upon earth.

PAFLNELLITES" V. Sir,—Judging from the " Examiner" of Saturday,Mr. John Ilampson, the Conservative agent of Warrington, must be a very touchy sort of fellow. It's all right to he touchy when a person really has cause for it, but in this case, as it somas to Me. Mr. Ilampo,n has only received back an equivalent for what he gave. lie's been served tit for tat, or got. qvid pro quo, and he can't hear being .• shown up." What is known no the Parnellite party consists of the iminediats followers of Mr. Parnell, and, although Liberals are not ashamed of their advocary of the mine principles of Home Rule for Ireland that Mr. Parnell is advocating, they have a perfect right to their own title ,d Liberals, and do well to maintain it. The Irish question is not the only qunition in politics, and what on earth it has to dr, in connection with the Wan rington Ward of thiardians I fail to see. The Pigott retort was simply Ilealing out to Mr. Hampron a peck from his own measure, and he would have shown won' wisdom if he had accepted his defeat without crying about it. His "dodge" NMI exposed, and it is only natural that he slimild not like the exposure, but a person in the position of a political agent should be aware that then. is danger in playing with edged tools. Ile has had his leikson ; that it may do lam gash is the wish of A LIBERAL. Warrington, April 3td, 1889.

AN INTERESTINI! INQUIRY. Sir,-1 am sure it would herd intenet to many of your readers to know in what part of the wooed Mr. !lamp- oon, the agent of the Warrington Conservative Associa- tion, was born anol reared. There is a naiveness and simplicity about Mr. Ilampson which is not fnund in any of the denizens of the countries of" advanced " civilitatiom, nor among the " heathen Chinee." Mr. Hampton is the paid agent of one political patty, and be calls the party to which his paymasters are opposed by another name than their own, and when this is corn. minted on he in effect says that be gave them this other name because he thought it would be acompliment. ' Now, Mr. !tampion knows SY will as everybody If se that he is not paid to compliment the other party. If he is paid for anything at all in that line it is not for invent- ing what is complimentary, but for inventing what he conceives to be une omplionentary. Hut the sweet simplicity id Mr. Hampson mom. in when he tries to make psople believe that his object was to flatter and not to offend. If he is really serious a ties, and not guilty of apiece of contemptible cant, I say that it at owl) becemes a matter of curious interest to know where he was born or reared. It must have been in some poetic Arcadia which has not yet been discovered by the traveller, nor visited by the tourist.—Yours truly,

Sir,—Fora great number of years I have been hoping that our representatives in Parliament wouldelose Public HOLM'S on Sundays. And who ? Well, you an., it looks ratter imeer to go out of a church or chaptjj straight into a Tavern, and though I possibly am different to the great majority I,f the [lnman Rae, I do get thirsty on Sunnktvs as much as on any natter dav ; and indeed, often: relish arink mere then tban at anv odler time, in cons, nutmeg of the dry sermon it boo been my fate to "grin : and bear." Well—as I avid befiwe—for decency's sake— I keepiny beer and whisky at home, anti there. seated, " happily in the bosom of a fine funnily" of girls and boys, I enjoy myself to my heart's content ; and, as " Example no totter than Precept," my darlings learn " How to do it," and in due course, will basso nut have done—and, porhaps onset m3.—and show in their lives the value of "Grandinclherly Legislation."

Yes, sir, we are-advmding 'last into a high state of civilisation. and shall soon have any amount of "filet. Life Below Stairs," lathe matter of &Ms at every other private house, when the Sunday will be made tin' princi- pal doe for dispensing the geed things "the gods have provided." And all this owing to " Grandmotherly Legislation," which will insist on making people good by Act Isf Parliament. We shall then find tin churches and chapels more thinly attended, because home, with the Bairns and the Beer, will be so much more attractive than the" holy howls" of rabid sectarian parsons, who fulminate against one of God's gifts, and preach as if , man were not a reasonable and a masoning being, and responsible to a higher Power, each individual one for himself.

'--71;:lianaties and " Faddists " argue that, bemuse, in places where the Public Houses are closed on Sundays, there are fewer drunkards to be seen about the town I than in those places where the houses are open, that. i therefore, theca is less drink ronsumed ! What a bourti. ful theory it is! It is mid though, that not even the stale jokes of Sir Wilfrid Lawson, nor tlielmnderousbuffoonery of that twilitical" Jumping Frog," Sir William Harcourt, ; can make it plain why it is so. But a person void of blinding bias can surely see that it is breattse the drink ' is consumed privately ; and that, in consequence, the police have less chance of judging correctly. Oh, far- toeing Legislators, who have carried the second Heading of the Sunday Closing Act; w,u nay succeed in foisting your "talon the Statute hook ; but from that dao private family drinking will increase, and your children will heroine more and more accustomed to the sight of a debauched Home and a neglected Sanetuary—to the unspeakable credit of" Grandmotherly Let,:islalion." %INDEX. That on Wednesday next, tit the Burial lioanl, Mr. I Colebum will probably again bring forward his motion as to tile illegality of using the mortuary as a place in which to make imxt more., examinations., Mr. Celeburn's reading of the law may be strictly accurate, but common sense would suggest that the mortuary is the proper place for slick surgical oper- ations, and it would he folly to put the ratepayers to the expense of constructing a buildlng that woitid not be used half-a-dozen times in twelve months.

That nowsa-days, with the multiplicity of building societies in the neighbourhood, no working-man who has a couple of chilling, a week to spare ought to be without a house of his own. The Economic Building Ssieiety was commenced at Widnes on Tuesday evening under favourable auspices, and a similar society is shortly to be formed in Runcorn. There are also four Starr Bowkett Societies (two at Runcorn and two at Whines), and one industrial society in existence, and these would seem to be more than adequate to supply the needs of the district for many years to come. May they all nourish.

That recently several members of our Runcorn Football Club have been placed hors de rombot through rough play on the field, and an Mee worthy the consideration of the Committee of the Club is suggested. In numerous towns successful classes are carried on under the auspices of the St. John's Ambulance Society, to the benefit of those who take advantage of them, and what would be more appro- priate than a class formed of members of the Foot- ball Club, with the addition, say, of our noble defenders the Volunteers. Or, Mangan, one of the ' enthusiastic patrons of the Football Club, would no doubt be glad to give the necessary lectures if approached on the subject, and the more students and the better.

Mr. Earp spoke in opponition, and seconded an amend- ment, but the original motion was carried. Matters still continue quiet on this section, ;trot the chief work carried on during the past week lias been pile driving in the river bed. A double row of huge piles now extends from underneath Runcorn Bridge past the ferry on to a point opposite the end of Belvedere, and the width and dirwtion of the river wall of the canal can easily be sumesed. On Tuesday afternoon a number of directors cf the Ship Canal ComPanY were in the town on busineva, and took advantage of the opportunity to view the wall constructed at Su Man's Land. 'limy were conducted aver the works by Mr. tiregson, the agent, and appeared surprised at the pro- gress that had been made with the river operations in Cu short a period. In the course of a week or no. the section will present the scene of nativity it did two mouths ago. •` •

div.p: THELWALL.

: A new bridge o.r the deviated course of the Mersey opposite Thelwail baS row been completed. It is a hand- -1 :sane and substantial structure, arid is a substitute for the ancient ferry that existed at Thelwall. In this neighbourhood the work of cutting the canal continues to progress at a great rate, and at night passengers on the trams that pass the works can see navvies busily engaged, the scene sf operations being lit up by a number of irelrs lights.

Another arm/lent, though not of a ',nous nature, occurred on the Thelwall section of the Ship Canal, on Saturday, when an elderly man named John Smith broke his ankle. Ile was conveyed to the hospital, where his injuritw were attended to by Dr. Byrne. THE CONTRACTOR AND DRINK.
Mr. Walker, contractor fWille 'Manchester Ship Canal, according to The Alliance News," has ordered that any of his men belonging to drinking clubs shall be dismissed from his employment._
il PRE-HISTORIC 'FIND.'

An interesting find" has been made this week on the Barton section of the Ship Canal Works, in the shape of a probably pre-("oinan canoe, hewn or burnt out of the solid trunk of an oak tree. The canoe was , turned up by a steam navvy in Salteyo cutting from a depth of 25 feet, along with a number of imbedded trees ' of immense circumference, which suggest the site of an ancient forest. A valuable specimeu of the pre-historic hand milbitone was recently unearthed at the same at and further revelations are being caret ally looked tor. The canoe, which is in remarkably gait] preservation, is 1311. fin, long, and some 18 inches deep inside, with a thickness of from 28in. to 3in. of wood. At Sticking's Island the remains of what have pronably been salt borings have his% found at a great depth. beneath the surface. A number of valuable fossils have also been found.

Manchester Examiuer ! andlimes" says i—Between Eastham and Manchester there is an almost unbrokencolumn of workmen 13,000 strong, and asthe summer advances the colutnn will become more compact until it numbers 20.000. Seem- ingly only a Mint could keep such a concern going, and it is not surprising to learn that no lexi than £30,000 a week for wages will both:Lien from the treasury of the Manehtster Ship Canal Company. Already the total capital expenditure of the commity since its formation has been about four and a half millions sterling, includ- ing the purchase of the Bridgewater Canahfor which was paid the sum of £1,710,000. Never before in the his Wry of English engineering enterprise has such an. enarmou.s plant been needed. Mr. Walker estimates its value at between £BOO,OOO and £700,000. DISASTER IN THE ENGLISH CHANNEL.

AN OSTEND MAIL BOAT BLOWN UP. On Saturday morning news was receiver,' that the Cointease de Plandre was rim into trv. the Belgian steamer Henrietta which froo crossing the Channel in an oppos- ite direction, and blew up immediately, killing the cap- tain said 14 others. Prince Leopold. of Belgium ss,s amongst those on bard, but escaped injury. His valet was one of the killed. Another Belgian mail packet arrived at the Admiralty pier, Dover' on Saturday inorn. lug, between seven:mit eight o'clock, and the captain of the vessel lab/tight full information with him 4 tiled's- aster which;had °enured. This, however, lin dobnel to give to any except the officials connected with the collision i—'line Conitesse de Flandre, which left Ostend with 20 passenger,' on her way to Dover, 'awe into Coi- lifion off Dunkirk with the steainpacket Prin.:so Henrietie, which had left Dover for Ostend that day with 15 passengers. The weather was thick at the time, and , ahnost diroetly after the vessels were sighted the culli- sion occurred. The Princess Ilenriette crushed into the ' Comte.. de Flambe, and her bow rnit through the paddle box and wheel, and penetrated into One engine room. The most terrible excitement followed. One part blew up and sank, and the other wart turned over and floated. A terrible scene was witnessed.. .

......- .........- -............ Captain Housemann was the commander of the Comtesse, with Lieutenant Verineulen an his chief mate, and the chief engineer, Mr. Martin. Every one in the engine room and stokeholes is supposed to have been blown up or drowned. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. IMPORTANT RULES FOR PLAINTIFFS. At the Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkea drew attention to rule 14 of order 23 in County Court rules, 1889, which is on follows :—" Where there is ati linsat is- lied judgment, or order. the plaintiff may apply es parte to the Court in which the same was given, Or made, to order that the amount due and unpaid, he paid by instalments, or, if payable by instalments, by like or snialler instalments, and the Court may there- open make an order accordingly." Ills Honour said that uniler the present practice, if a person Was brought lip ova judgment suinmons for an amount which is , beyond his pnwer to pay within a reasonable time, the only result was that a fresh order was made to pay so moch per month. Thk involved considerable waste of titer and trouble and expense en the lout of the plaintiff and tone and trouble on the part of the 0111 d and on the part of the defendant, who so nit to appear hi answ, to the summons. In order to obviate this, the new rule had been made and Inn' hoped the plaintiffs WOUld avail themselves of it largely. Under this rule the plaintiff nisol not summons the defendant. If the plaintiff wa.s satisfied that the inert. of the defendant were such that he could not pay the amount ordered all at otwe, he might apply to the registrar at the Comity Court office, or to the judge, to make the order payable hy such instalments as lie theoght tlyi defendant coedit make. Or supposing the jutlontrnt is payabl.. by instalments, then the plaintiff could make an applicationthat it may be paid in smaller instalments. The object of that Wan this Supposing a man orderol to pay Si. or Is. per month had for some re.on or ether fallen into arrears to the extent of 20s. or 30s, and the plaintiff well knew that the inan could not may the money, it worild therefore be a wise thing on the loft of the plaintiff to obtain a fresh order for the instahnents to begin again. div.head: MR. JOHN BRIGHT AT PENKETII.
div.p: MR. JOHN BRIGHT AT PENKETII.

A circumstance of a good deal of local, and at the present time of not a little general interest, seems to have escaped the notice of all the numerous biographers of the late Mr. John Bright, and it is that the great tribune " received part of his education at the Friends School at the village of ' Penketh, near Warrington. It would probably be about the year lAN when Mr. Bright, as a lad of thirteen or fourteen years, was at Penketh School, which WWI at that time kept by a person of the name of Joseph Edmondson. The school at that time was carried oil in the old school near the Meeting Iloust•, and not in the present school building. Among the pupils who were taught at the school along with Mr. Bright wan the late Mr. Samuel Broadhurst, of Great Sankey. While at Penketh, Mr. Bright lodged with Mr..). Davies in a house which is still standing. Mr. l'eter Davies, a son of the Mr. Davies with whom Mr. Bright lived,' anti of about the same age as Mr. Bright, lives near Newry,in Ireland. and Miss Davies, of Penketh, is a sister of thin gentleman. A younger brother of Mt. Bright—Mr. Benjamin Bright —was, later on, educated at the some school at Penketh and by the same master, Alderman Holmes, of Warrington, being a contemporary scholar of this youngest brother cf Mr. Bright.

Snooty.: DOMESTIC TNAGEOV.—A domestic tragedy is reported from notion.la. near Portadown. Two brothers, named M.tigymn. on going home, found their! father drunk and their mother turned out. They warned I their father that he must give up hi, drinking habits. and he retorted with threats and struck at them with a rake. One of them seised a crook and cut open his father's head with a blow, which proved fatal. SMOCK". Aconywr TO A Sr. HELENS Docrow—On Friday morning Dr. Edward P. Twyford, magistrate for the beroug,ll of St. Helens, and a county justice, was 4riving in an optn otrriage on his morning round to patients, and, when croasing the railway bridge near Parr Church, the horse took fright at an engine shunting. Dr. Twyford, attempting to get out, was thrown heavily to the ground, fractured several rit., and received injury to the skull and onicu,sion of the brain. Ilia condition ! is very serious.

...... - THE TAM NATION Aces. —On the motion for going into Supply,Mr. Pice movisl a public 3/14.11VHS to the Crown, praying for the appointment of a Royal Commission to inquire into the way Vaccination Acts we., adminis- tered. He also desired an inquiry.., regarded the pre- valence of smallpox, or otherwise, in any towns or districts in which the Guardians had for two years or mini failed to prosecute for refusal to vaccinate, and likewise into the system of compulsory notification, isolation, and quarantine as carried out in Leicester, and elsewhere, and that the Royal Commissions should take evidemy as to present slate of scientific and medical opinion on the effect of vaccination where such existed. and further. that they should report whether any change In the law was in their opinion desirable. Ile condemned the system in force as an outrage 01 the consciences of people, and cited numbers of cases where vaccination hail fatally failed. To show an instanee against com- pulsory vaccination, he gave the case of a prtir man who, in less than four years, had been fined for not romplying with the law .37 times. the p.como amount of fines amounting to no 11.8.4 than DEG as. 63.—Fir. rer- amen,: seconded Mr. Pictim'sproposal Weans., he wished inquiry should take place, feeling sure vaccination would come out triumphant and strengthened—Mr. Ritchie, whilA strenuously defending vaccination, insisted that countries where vaccination laws were strongest were freest from smallpox. The Government, however, had decided to appoints Royal Commissi.m.—Sir li. Hunter was gratified that the Government had decided to appoint a Royal Commission. He believed that every unvacci- nated person was a source of danger to the people.—Mr. T. Robinson, Mr. Stansfield, Sir J. Pease, Dr. Cameron, and others exprerted gratification that a Rival Commis- RlOll was to be appointed.—Mr. Picton wished to withdraw his proposal, but it WHS negatived WithOU, a division. The house was counted out at eight o'clock.
